Stimuli-responsive hydrogels are promising materials as they undergo reversible swelling and shrinkage when exposed to external stimuli, thereby enabling changes in reactor geometry and flow conditions. However, their low mechanical stability limits their use as structural reactor elements. This paper therefore proposes a multi-material additive manufacturing approach combining material extrusion of thermoplastics with a second extrusion system for hydrogel precursor. Hydrogel formulations with different water contents are investigated regarding printability and curing behavior, and response surface methodology is used to identify a robust processing parameter set. The selected formulation exhibits an average mass-based shrinkage of 54.22 ± 3.36% between 25 and 40 °C, while image-based measurements show that the majority of the volume change occurs within the first 5–10 min, with an apparent volumetric plateau reached after 16–18 min. Thermoresponsive actuation is further demonstrated using hydrogel-thermoplastic polyurethane bilayer specimens, with all specimens exhibiting a complete reversal in bending direction and curvature changes between 0.0343 and 0.0550 mm⁻¹. Based on these results, potential hydrogel-polymer design elements for smart reactors are proposed, including adaptive baffles, variable flow cross-sections, flow redirecters, and adaptive structured reactor internals.

articles.title: A physics-guided graph neural framework for real-time reconstruction of mechanical microenvironments in engineered cartilage scaffolds
articles.abstract: The spatially heterogeneous mechanical microenvironment within engineered cartilage scaffolds critically regulates cell fate and extracellular matrix maturation, yet its real-time characterization remains limited by the computational burden of high-fidelity finite element analysis (FEA) simulations. This study develops Phys-MRGNet, a topology-conditioned physics-guided graph neural network that rapidly reconstructs the mechanical microenvironment of a 3D-printed cartilage scaffold under varying material states and loading conditions. The network was trained on finite-element simulation sequences spanning an experimentally constrained viscoelastic parameter domain of the scaffold, with short, medium, and long edges modeled as distinct mechanical relations and a graph-Laplacian-based mechanical field consistency regularizer without extra learnable parameters. On 20 independently held-out FEA sequences comprising 4.55 × 106 node-step predictions, the model achieved coefficients of determination of 0.9806 and 0.9805 for interior and domain-boundary constitutive states, and a 9% lower hotspot-edge deviation than the variant without the physical term. Inference takes approximately 0.1 s per sequence, roughly 1.2 × 103 times faster than batch FEA on our hardware. Phys-MRGNet reproduces finite-element strain fields with high accuracy and enables rapid screening of mechanical conditioning strategies for engineered cartilage maturation through a Unity3D digital-proxy prototype, providing a mechanically relevant field descriptor for mechanobiological analysis of scaffold culture.

articles.title: Computational Investigations on Viability of Inorganic Cs 2 AgBiI 6 Double Perovskite Semiconductor for Hybrid Solar Cell Modules
articles.abstract: The structural, electronic, and optical properties of lead-free double perovskite Cs2AgBiI6 were investigated using density functional theory (DFT) within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) implemented in Quantum ESPRESSO. Cs2AgBiI6 exhibits an indirect band gap, with the valence band maximum and conduction band minimum located at different high-symmetry points. Structural stability was assessed using convex hull analysis and the Goldschmidt tolerance factor, while optical calculations revealed strong visible-light absorption. The obtained material parameters were subsequently employed to design a hybrid solar cell with the configuration Au/Spiro-OMeTAD/Cs2AgBiI6/CIGS/CdS/TiO2/FTO using SCAPS-1D. The optimized device achieved a power conversion efficiency of 44.86%, with an open-circuit voltage of 1.092 V, short-circuit current density of 49.98 mA/cm2, and fill factor of 82.11%. PVsyst simulations yielded a maximum module power of 1025.9 W at 1000 W/m2 irradiance, demonstrating the potential of Cs2AgBiI6 for efficient lead-free photovoltaics.

articles.title: Physics-informed gradient boosting regression tree for tool wear prediction in milling
articles.abstract: Accurate prediction of tool flank wear is critical for maintaining machining quality, minimizing unplanned downtime, and enabling condition-based tool replacement. Data-driven models may violate physical wear laws under limited or varying data, whereas mechanistic models often lack the flexibility to capture complex, nonlinear wear evolution. To bridge this gap, this study proposes a physics-informed gradient boosting regression tree (PIGBRT) approach that integrates the generalized tool wear degradation law into the GBRT learning framework. In this method, the physical degradation law is formulated as a regularization term and integrated with the conventional data loss to construct a composite objective function, thereby jointly enforcing data fidelity and physical consistency during model training. The regression trees are then iteratively constructed along the negative gradient of the composite loss, enabling the physical prior to continuously constrain the learning trajectory rather than being imposed only during post-processing. Experimental validation on milling datasets demonstrates that the proposed PIGBRT achieves accurate tool wear prediction, with superior generalization and physical consistency compared with purely data-driven, mechanistic, and other advanced methods. These results highlight the effectiveness of embedding explicit physical knowledge into ensemble learning and establish PIGBRT as a promising framework for physics-consistent and generalizable tool monitoring in milling processes.

articles.title: Three-dimensional volumetric characterization of CFRP surface integrity in milling: comparison with conventional roughness parameters
articles.abstract: Machined surface quality in carbon fibre reinforced polymer (CFRP) is commonly assessed using roughness parameters, which may not fully represent heterogeneous three-dimensional topography. This study investigates whether volumetric descriptors complement profile and areal roughness in milled CFRP surfaces. Dry up-milling experiments were conducted using a two-flute polycrystalline diamond end mill under a full factorial design with cutting speeds of 200 and 300 m/min and feed per tooth values of 0.017, 0.033 and 0.050 mm/tooth. Surface quality was characterized by focus-variation optical metrology using Ra, Sa, Above Surface Volume and Below Surface Volume. Cutting force, final cutting-edge radius and selected µCT observations supported interpretation of the machining response. Two-way ANOVA showed that feed per tooth accounted for 84.1% of Ra variation, while cutting speed and its interaction with feed were not significant. In contrast, Sa and both volumetric descriptors were significantly affected by cutting speed, feed and their interaction. At 0.050 mm/tooth, increasing cutting speed from 200 to 300 m/min changed Ra only from 1.527 to 1.426 µm, whereas the response shifted from above-surface dominated (Vabove = 0.975 mm³, Vbelow = 0.033 mm³) to below-surface dominated (Vabove = 0.106 mm³, Vbelow = 0.231 mm³). The 300 m/min condition exhibited more numerous and extensive µCT-visible discontinuities than the 200 m/min condition. Analysis over cumulative cutting length showed no universal monotonic relationship between cutting force and surface quality. Overall, the separated volumetric descriptors complement Ra and Sa by retaining the direction of three-dimensional topographic deviation, providing additional information for CFRP machining-quality assessment.

articles.title: Plant Growth–Promoting Potential of Endophytic Bacteria Isolated from Asparagus racemosus Willd and their role in improving Chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.) Germination
articles.abstract: Endophytic bacteria inhabiting internal plant tissues are increasingly recognized for their role in enhancing plant growth and stress tolerance. The present study investigated the plant growth-promoting potential of root-associated endophytic bacteria isolated from the medicinal plant Asparagus racemosus Willd. and evaluated their effect on seed germination of desi chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.). Healthy tuberous roots were surface sterilized, and endophytic bacteria were isolated using standard microbiological techniques. Seven morphologically distinct bacterial isolates were obtained and characterized through morphological, biochemical, and molecular approaches. The isolates were screened for important plant growth-promoting traits including indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) production, phosphate solubilization, nitrogen fixation, siderophore production, ammonia production, hydrogen cyanide production, ACC deaminase activity, and extracellular hydrolytic enzymes. Among the isolates, strain AR1 exhibited the most comprehensive PGP profile, showing positive responses for IAA production, phosphate solubilization, nitrogen fixation, siderophore production, ACC deaminase activity, and multiple hydrolytic enzymes. Molecular identification based on 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that AR1 belonged to Enterobacter wuhouensis, while amplification of the nifH gene confirmed its nitrogen-fixing potential. Seed inoculation experiments demonstrated a substantial enhancement in chickpea germination, with inoculated seeds achieving 85.19% germination compared to 29.63% in uninoculated controls. Enhanced radicle growth and seedling vigor were also observed. These findings highlight A. racemosus as a valuable reservoir of beneficial endophytic bacteria and demonstrate the potential of strain AR1 as a bioinoculant for sustainable crop production. Further investigations involving whole-genome sequencing, transcriptomic analyses, and multilocation field evaluations are warranted to validate its agricultural applicability under diverse environmental conditions.

articles.title: THz Calorimetry of Electrolyte Solutions Links Water's H-Bond Network to Macroscopic Properties
articles.abstract: Understanding the macroscopic properties of aqueous electrolyte solutions over their full solubility range requires a detailed microscopic picture of water-ion interactions. We combine THz calorimetry and dimensionality-reduction tech- niques to demonstrate that two to four spectroscopic markers are sufficient to describe ion-specific variations in mixing entropies and enthalpies, viscos- ity, and limiting conductivity across 19 electrolytes. Those markers allow us to classify electrolytes as ’strong’ or ’weak’ and report on changes in the water’s H-bond network. As concentration increases, spectroscopic nonlinearities due to ion aggregation appear that, based on a multipole expansion model for activi- ties, are correlated with density changes. For CsI and LiCl, as prototypes of weak and strong electrolytes, respectively, the multipole expansion model accurately describes their conductivities, viscosities, and surface tensions. THz spectroscopy in combination with an activity coefficient model directly correlates macroscopic solution properties with changes in the H-bond network, paving the way towards efficient machine-learning approaches.

articles.title: The Price of Non-Hermiticity: Exact Stability, Dissipation, and Isolation Bounds for Passive Nonreciprocal Electrical Networks
articles.abstract: Electrical circuits realize non-Hermitian tight-binding models node by node, but which of them a circuit can actually realize, and at what cost, has not been made quantitative. This paper casts circuit realizability as an inverse problem over three layers--an admissible network class, a frequency-window ˝ngerprint, and resource functionals (component count, dissipation, bandwidth, stability margin, isolation, and throughput)�and solves its one-dimensional instance exactly. Positive-real theory separates the passivity gap from the stability gap: the stability threshold of a nonreciprocal chain is a surface-state value strictly smaller than the usually quoted bulk band edge, and it vanishes for the conservative split. Skin localization in a passive cir-cuit exists but is not free: a passive modulus-changing bond must dissipate a minimum conductance, and isolation is an exact identity that survives ar-bitrary bond disorder. A complete, tabletop-ready experimental design in the audio band is provided; all closed forms are validated numerically, and component values are specfied.

articles.title: Chirality of 'trions' illuminates new paths for quantum optics
articles.abstract: Scientists from Tokyo Metropolitan University have discovered that charged states made of two electrons and a positively charged hole (or vice versa) on atomically thin rolls of carbon atoms have a structure-derived "handedness" in how they interact with light. While electron-hole pairs, or "excitons," were known to keep the chirality of the underlying nanotube, the team showed that adding a charge to create "trions" does not change this property.

articles.title: Variational quantum principal component analysis for Hilbert space Gaussian process regression
articles.abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) are widely used probabilistic models for regression and classification tasks. Their flexibility and ability to quantify uncertainties make them well-suited for many applications. However, their applicability to large datasets is limited by the cubic computational time complexity. While reduced-rank methods such as Hilbert space approximations reduce this complexity, scaling to very large datasets remains challenging. Quantum algorithms are promising candidates to further accelerate such computations. Quantum principal component analysis (QPCA) has previously been applied to Hilbert space GP (HSGP) regression to address this scaling limitation. However, its applicability is limited by the requirement for fault-tolerant quantum hardware. In this work, we present a hybrid quantum–classical model for reduced-rank GP regression, where we apply a QPCA algorithm based on parameterized quantum circuits to HSGP regression. In noiseless simulations on a one-dimensional test function, the resulting model reaches a regression accuracy comparable to that of the exact GP and the classical HSGP. The framework uses shallow parameterized circuits and does not require fault-tolerant quantum hardware, which makes it a candidate for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

articles.title: Nonequilibrium Fluctuations and Intrinsic Stability of Nanostructured Solar Cells: Microscopic Derivation and Universal Laws
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study nonequilibrium fluctuations of efficiency in nanostructured solar cells. Our contribution is threefold. First, we derive a microscopic stochastic model of efficiency from a two-state master equation describing absorption, radiative recombination, and extraction. This derivation establishes an explicit link between efficiency fluctuations and entropy production, and justifies the thermodynamic affinity through local detailed balance. Second, we review universal fluctuation laws established in the recent literature and apply them for the first time to the real parameters of nanostructured solar cells. We show that the total entropy production behaves as a submartingale, and that its negative exponential is a martingale. For a biased discrete random walk, the exact infimum law is verified numerically in the near-equilibrium regime, then applied to realistic solar cell configurations. Third, our simulations show that nanostructured solar cells operate in a strongly nonequilibrium regime, where negative entropy fluctuations, and hence efficiency fluctuations, are exponentially rare. Over all simulated trajectories, most configurations show no detectable negative fluctuation, consistent with the theoretical prediction. These results explain the intrinsic statistical stability of the devices and provide a conceptual and quantitative framework for understanding efficiency fluctuations around the mean values. They do not modify the mean efficiencies obtained previously, but clarify their statistical robustness in the strongly nonequilibrium regime.

articles.title: Experimental realization of twofold topological phase transition induced by long-range hoppings in one-dimensional chains
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-range hoppings offer a powerful mechanism to engineer exotic topological phases beyond conventional tight-binding models. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a twofold topological phase transition driven by third-nearest-neighbor couplings in a one-dimensional phononic chain that emulates cis-polyacetylene. Tunable hopping parameters in highly structured aluminum plates allow us to observe the emergence of Dirac points, a valley pseudospin structure, and topological edge states. The experimental results are supported by non-equilibrium Green's function transport calculations. Our findings confirm the predicted long-range phase diagram and establish phononic metamaterials as a versatile platform for exploring topological phenomena beyond the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger paradigm.

articles.title: Disentangling Multiple Scaling Dimensions via Operator Covariance in Critical Quantum Spin Systems
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a general proof of different power-law decays versus distance of the eigenvalues of two-point covariance matrices in critical lattice quantum models, allowing extraction of multiple scaling dimensions. We demonstrate the practical utility of this method in the context of a spin-1/2 chain with critical ground state described by the SU(2)₁ Wess--Zumino--Witten field theory. Using quantum Monte Carlo simulations to compute covariance matrices in different symmetry sectors, we resolve the expected relevant and marginal primary operators as well as some descendants. The covariance method can be integrated into many existing numerical schemes and promises to significantly enhance computational studies of quantum criticality.

articles.title: Analytical mean-field model for electrochemical metallization memristors with a nanoporous matrix: application to Ag/anodic alumina/Al
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memristors based on electrochemical metallization with many filaments are usually modeled by microscopic simulations with many parameters or by phenomenological laws whose parameters are hard to relate to physical quantities. We present an analytical mean-field model for a population of Ag filaments confined in the pores of a nanoporous matrix, built on Ohm's law, Faraday's law and a power-based rupture criterion. The filaments have a truncated normal distribution of cross-sections and rupture leaving lognormally distributed gaps whose median grows with the dissipated power. Gap closing shifts the distribution of squared gaps rigidly, and the model therefore admits closed-form expressions for the switching voltage, the read current, the rupture branch and the high-voltage current. We apply it to Ag/nanoporous anodic alumina/Al structures fabricated from industrial-grade aluminum, with a 2.4μm alumina layer, and measured under ambient conditions. The parameters were fitted to the bipolar sweeps, with the gap dispersion taken from the temporal shape of the read after a pulse. They reproduce the bipolar response, including voltage-controlled negative differential resistance, and predict without refitting the unipolar sweeps and the amplitude of the pulse response, where state memory appears. A second sample, with a larger contact deposited chemically, is described by the same model. In vacuum the devices neither switch nor show negative differential resistance, as expected if adsorbed water supplies the counter reaction; the residual high-voltage current follows ionic hopping conduction.

articles.title: Evaporation-induced colloidal diffusiophoresis in electrolyte solutions
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-volatile solutes accumulate near a receding drying front, generating concentration gradients that can drive directional colloidal transport by diffusiophoresis. This dynamic spatial arrangement of colloidal particles could affect the microstructure and macroscopic properties of the dried film. Here, we combine experiments and theory to investigate polystyrene particles suspended in electrolyte solutions drying within a capillary tube. By varying the electrolyte composition and ambient relative humidity, we show that evaporation-induced ion gradients drive particles toward the liquid-gas interface and enhance interfacial accumulation, whereas slower drying at higher humidity weakens the gradient and particle migration. We use the heat balance integral method to predict the transient solute field for a receding interface and couple it to particle transport to capture the observed particle trajectories and accumulation trends. These results identify background electrolytes and drying rate as coupled controls on particle distribution and provide a predictive framework to optimize formulation and processing parameters for manufacturing slurry-based materials, such as battery electrodes and turbine coatings.

articles.title: Strong phonon-coupled trion emission in Janus homobilayer
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Janus transition metal dichalcogenides with broken mirror symmetry provide a novel platform for exploring many-body effects mediated by spin-valley-phonon interactions. Strong electron-phonon coupling demands a precise match between a strong effective dipole moment and nanometer-scale charge confinement. Here, we report thermally robust and enhanced trion emission in a symmetric bilayer WSeS with an S/S stacking configuration. The inward-pointing antiparallel built-in electric fields induce a strong electron confinement effect at the interface, driving dominant trion emission at cryogenic temperatures. Furthermore, a massive electron-phonon coupling strength (3.9) resonant with the optical phonon A₁² energy (51 meV) contributes to the thermal stability of this trion emission at elevated temperatures. By tailoring the interfacial architecture in Janus WSeS homobilayers, this study overcomes the thermal decoherence limits inherent to traditional semiconductor systems, offering novel insights into room-temperature many-body interactions.

articles.title: Spontaneous Formation of Lateral Defect-Density Gradient in CVD-Grown MoS2 Monolayers
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Defect engineering in two-dimensional materials is a powerful strategy for tuning electronic, optical, and catalytic properties. While pristine molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) has been thoroughly studied, defective MoS2 remains poorly understood due to the complexity and inconsistency of controlled defect creation. Here, we report a defect-density gradient that forms spontaneously in MoS2 flakes during chemical vapor deposition (CVD) growth. Photoluminescence and Raman spectroscopy mapping reveal the lateral arrangement of this gradient across a single flake. Deconvolution of the excitonic photoluminescence emission identifies electron doping as the key factor governing the spatial variation in optical response. This doping likely originates from sulfur vacancies formed during CVD growth, as further supported by the observed Raman mode shifts. We propose that this gradient arises from precursor depletion near the nucleation center during growth, resulting in a gradual variation in defect density. This lateral defect structure provides a convenient platform for systematically characterizing defective MoS2 across a continuous range of defect densities within a single sample. The sulfur-vacancy-driven surface activation identified here can also be important for future catalytic applications.

articles.title: A Monte Carlo study of thermal conductivity in black phosphorene
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09149v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work the electronic thermal conductivity of black phosphorene is studied. Using the Monte Carlo method together with the Green-Kubo relations, a statistical modelling of the motion and scattering of electrons on acoustic and optical phonons is performed to estimate the electronic thermal conductivity. The scattering probability is expressed analytically. The obtained results show a pronounced anisotropy of the thermal conductivity: the thermal conductivity values along the armchair direction are an order of magnitude larger than those along the zigzag direction, in agreement with the experimental data for related materials. In addition, the modelling allowed a more rigorous justification of some results of previous theoretical works on the anisotropic thermal conductivity of black phosphorene.

articles.title: Lefschetz-Thimble Method to the Sign Problem in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev Model
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The sign problem in path integrals severely limits the application of quantum Monte Carlo methods to strongly correlated systems, whereas the Lefschetz-thimble method offers a rigorous framework to mitigate this issue. In this paper, we establish a numerical framework based on the Lefschetz thimbles for the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model. By introducing continuous auxiliary fields via the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, the partition function is formulated as a high-dimensional complex integral. We employ the complex Langevin equation to explore the saddle-point distribution of the effective action in the complex plane. Monte Carlo integration is then performed to compute the partition function and Green functions. Our numerical results exhibit excellent agreement with high-temperature expansions, infrared-limit solutions, and determinantal quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) simulations, confirming the validity of our framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our complex Langevin search successfully captures the relevant dominant saddle points governing the SYK model in the large-N limit. Our work deepens the understanding of the sign problem in the SYK model and provides a viable non-perturbative avenue for addressing sign problems in more complex strongly correlated systems.

articles.title: A Compact High-Repetition-Rate Intense THz Source for Atomic-Scale Materials Characterization
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-intensity terahertz (THz) sources combining high repetition rates, strong field amplitudes, and long-term stability are key enabling technologies for next-generation ultrafast photonics. However, simultaneously achieving these characteristics in a compact and practical architecture remains a major challenge. Here, we report a high-performance tabletop THz source delivering intense single-cycle pulses at 100 kHz, generated by optical rectification in lithium niobate using an optimized echelon-based tilted-pulse-front scheme and driven by an industrial-grade ytterbium laser. The source achieves optical-to-THz conversion efficiencies exceeding 0.13% at room temperature, peak electric fields of several hundred kV/cm, and excellent long-term stability, establishing a robust platform for high-average-power strong-field THz applications. As a proof of concept, the source was integrated into an atom probe tomography (APT) instrument. APT reconstructs the three-dimensional chemical composition of materials through field-induced ion emission from a sharp nanotip. While THz-assisted ion emission has been shown to improve analytical performance by reducing thermal effects, previous demonstrations were limited to low-repetition-rate THz sources, restricting throughput and accessible analysis volumes. Using an aluminum nanotip, we demonstrate efficient THz-assisted APT at 100 kHz and benchmark its performance against conventional voltage- and laser-assisted operation. The high repetition rate enables rapid large-volume acquisition while improving mass resolving power, reducing thermal tailing, and preserving high-quality three-dimensional reconstructions. Beyond APT, this work establishes a compact and scalable high-repetition-rate THz platform for strong-field physics, nonlinear THz photonics, ultrafast spectroscopy, and material characterization at the nanoscale.

articles.title: Momentum-space engineering in van der Waals heterostructures
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Twenty years of graphene research have established Dirac fermions as a versatile platform for exploring quantum topological phenomena. Yet control over graphene's low-energy spectrum mostly follows the route of miniband engineering using real-space superlattices. Here we introduce a complementary approach based on momentum-space 'Umklapp' band engineering. This is realised by matching reciprocal space positions of band edges of two adjacent highly incommensurate 2D crystals to coincide upon a boost from their Bragg vectors, creating resonant interlayer hybridisation that qualitatively reconstructs their spectra. To demonstrate this approach experimentally, we use monolayer graphene on MoS₂, twisted such that MoS₂ Q-valley states are brought by Umklapp into energy-momentum resonance with graphene's Dirac cones. The ensuing hybridization results in the formation of a clear additional Dirac-like spectral feature, identified by a distinct Landau-level fan and Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations characteristic to Berry phase π electrons. These new topological spectral features create a spin-valley locked Ising system which is robust against small twist-angle variations that can be further tuned by an external displacement field. More broadly, Umklapp band engineering offers a practical strategy for tailoring the electronic structure in van der Waals heterostructures, expanding the design space of quantum materials beyond moiré superlattices and weak proximity effects.

articles.title: Stacking, symmetry and exciton fine structure in boron nitride bilayers
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09473v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Engineering of two-dimensional material heterostructures offers a broad range of degrees of freedom through the selection of type and number of layers and their relative stacking configurations. In these compound materials, the stacking sequence plays a central role in determining electronic, mechanical, and optical properties. Here, we present a theoretical study of its signature on the excitons of hexagonal boron nitride bilayers based on first-principle calculations within the GW approximation and the Bethe-Salpeter equation. We explain how stacking-dependent symmetry variations lead to distinct electronic structures, particularly near the band edge around the K high-symmetry point, and consequently to markedly different excitonic landscapes. Indeed, we analyze the symmetry-governed character of the low-lying excitonic states, identifying their bright or dark nature for each stacking configuration and performing a systematic comparison. Our results clarify how van der Waals interlayer coupling reshapes excitons in hexagonal boron nitride bilayers and outline prospects for twist-controlled exciton engineering in this material.

articles.title: Scanning Probe Control, Quantum Dynamics, and Dispersive Readout of Suspended Carbon Nanotube Resonators
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Suspended carbon nanotubes (CNTs) offer promising opportunities for quantum nanomechanics owing to their small effective mass, strong electrostatic tunability, and mechanical nonlinearity. We develop a unified theoretical framework for coherent control and readout of a suspended CNT driven by an atomic force microscope (AFM) tip and capacitively coupled to a Cooper-pair box (CPB). We first derive the linear and nonlinear Duffing response of the CNT and quantify the effects of AFM force gradients, tip-position fluctuations, and voltage noise on mechanical stability, dephasing, and heating. These results establish operating conditions for coherent actuation with limited backaction. We then quantize the Duffing oscillator, derive its Kerr anharmonicity, and identify the requirements for selective control of individual vibrational transitions. Estimates of thermal occupation and active cooling illustrate the constraints for CNT modes spanning frequencies from 54 MHz to 5.37 GHz. Finally, we derive the CNT--CPB interaction and its dispersive limit, showing how phonon number and parity can be mapped onto the CPB through Ramsey interferometry and detected using quantum-capacitance readout. The resulting framework identifies the conditions under which localized AFM actuation, nonlinear quantum dynamics, and superconducting state-resolved detection can operate within a single CNT device.

articles.title: Inversion symmetry breaking by interlayer hybridization in a tetralayer van der Waals heterostructure
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inversion symmetry breaking unlocks a broad range of physical phenomena fundamental for modern technologies, motivating efforts to engineer noncentrosymmetric materials. In this context, monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides, which naturally lack inversion symmetry, have emerged as a versatile platform for valley physics, strong excitonic effects, and nonlinear optics. However, in their hexagonal stacking phase, inversion symmetry is restored in even-layer stacks and bulk form, suppressing these effects and limiting applications. In this work, inversion symmetry breaking is demonstrated in a vertically stacked tetralayer heterostructure assembled from two intrinsically centrosymmetric bilayer flakes, as evidenced by second harmonic generation measurements with an intensity comparable to that of their constituent monolayer. Spectroscopic measurements and theoretical estimations indicate that effective symmetry breaking in the tetralayer heterostructure is driven by interlayer hybridization, giving rise to pronounced electronic and phononic signatures. This symmetry breaking further induces polar anisotropy, with an intensity ratio reaching 2.36. We propose that asymmetric contributions from excitons to the second harmonic optical dipole may influence this behavior. These findings establish interlayer coupling as a critical mechanism for introducing inversion symmetry breaking and tuning the optical response of van der Waals heterostructures, providing a powerful strategy for photonics and optoelectronics in two-dimensional materials.

articles.title: Experimental Evaluation of High-Throughput Structure Predictions
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High throughput computational databases such as Materials Project, the Open Quantum Materials Database, and Alexandria now each list on the order of 10⁵ predicted stable compounds. However, the overall reliability of these predictions in terms of actual experimental synthesizability remains poorly understood. In this work we attempt to synthesize, via arc melting, 34 different predicted ternary compounds. The majority of these materials did not form in the predicted structure, instead resulting in disordered variants or multiphase mixtures. Four formed ordered structures not reported before, one of them at a composition reported earlier without a structure. We discuss both the failures and the successes, and identify simple filtering criteria that can help researchers avoid hypothetical materials that are unlikely to form.

articles.title: Influenza A Virus as a Multivalent Active Particle: Statistical Mechanics of Binding, Motility, and Antiviral Design
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this contribution, we review existing multivalent models of Influenza A Virus (IAV) systems to study virion dynamics and design of multivalent entry blockers. We review existing biochemical estimations of the dissociation constants and catalytic activities of the two virion ligands [hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA)], which can be used to develop quantitative theories and experiments. Multivalent models are statistical mechanics frameworks for studying the simultaneous interaction of multiple reversible ligand-receptor bonds. They quantify the effects of both combinatorial entropy terms and single-molecule ligand-receptor affinities. Multivalent frameworks led to the rationale of superselectivity, the ability of probes to sense specific concentrations of conjugated receptors. Multivalent models guided the design of antiviral nanomedicines constituted by polymeric scaffolds conjugated with small molecules such as sialic acid receptors targeting the ligands on the surface of the virion. Importantly, neuraminidase is an enzyme that limits the number of host-guest bonds through receptor desialylation. Like active particles, neuraminidase activity enhances virion motility in the extracellular medium. Modeling the dynamics of Influenza A virions requires developing out-of-equilibrium multivalent models.

articles.title: Cavity-enhanced second harmonic generation from Rydberg excitons in Cu₂O
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rydberg excitons in Cu₂O provide a solid-state setting for creating giant optical nonlinearities. Here, we use second-harmonic generation (SHG) to study Rydberg excitons in a doubly resonant optical microcavity designed to enhance both the pump and second-harmonic fields. We observe even-parity exciton states in an optical cavity and extend cavity-based measurements of Rydberg excitons up to n=10. The SHG intensity depends strongly on pump cavity detuning, showing the dominant role of the microcavity is the enhancement of the intra-cavity pump field. Analysis reveals an additional enhancement from the resonant second-harmonic cavity giving an overall SHG enhancement factor of 21 ± 2 inside the microcavity. These results establish cavity-enhanced SHG spectroscopy as a valuable tool for studying Rydberg excitons in microcavities and provide a pathway towards exploiting optical nonlinearities in Rydberg exciton polariton systems.

articles.title: Microscopic theory of exciton polarons in transition metal dichalcogenides
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polarons are composite quasiparticles formed when charge carriers strongly couple to lattice vibrations, manifesting as carriers dressed by a surrounding cloud of phonons. Although this dressing fundamentally renormalizes the effective mass and mobility of carriers, its impact on electrically neutral exciton polarons in 2D semiconductors has received limited attention. In particular, despite the growing interest in polaronic effects in atomically thin semiconductors, only a few theoretical studies have addressed spectral signatures and renormalized properties of exciton polarons in these materials. Here, we develop a microscopic model to describe exciton polarons in transition metal dichalcogenides. Applying this model to 1s acoustic polarons in an MoSe₂ monolayer, we reveal a distinct kink in the polaron dispersion, accompanied by a pronounced broadening of its spectral function. These spectral signatures mark a critical transition from a regime of well-defined bound exciton polarons, characterized by a renormalized energy, reduced group velocity, and enhanced effective mass, to a regime dominated by exciton-phonon scattering. Furthermore, by incorporating intervalley exciton-phonon interaction, we demonstrate that the energetic position of momentum-dark excitons strongly modifies the exciton-polaron lifetime. Overall, our work provides a microscopic framework for determining renormalized properties of exciton polarons and establishes experimentally accessible polaron signatures in 2D semiconductors.

articles.title: Energy- and momentum-resolved Cooper-pair emission from a cuprate superconductor
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Superconductivity arises from Cooper pairing, but conventional photoemission probes electrons individually rather than as pairs. Here we report the observation of Cooper-pair emission from an optimally doped cuprate superconductor using two-electron angle-resolved photoemission (2e-ARPES). Below the superconducting transition, we observe a distinct two-electron emission peak at zero pair binding energy and zero pair momentum that disappears in the normal state, revealing the characteristic fingerprint of a Cooper pair. Unexpectedly, the joint energy distribution broadens markedly along the relative-energy axis as temperature decreases, while the total energy width remains nearly unchanged. This anomalous behavior cannot be explained by instrumental resolution, static disorder or thermal broadening, and instead points to scattering processes involving collective excitations of the superconductor. Our results establish 2e-ARPES as a probe of both Cooper-pair emission and the many-body dynamics of the superconducting state.

articles.title: Trajectory-Dependent Decoherence and Leakage During Shuttling of Multi-Spin Qubits
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Logical qubits encoded in collective states of multiple spins are promising building blocks for large-scale semiconductor quantum processors. As novel fault-tolerant architectures increasingly rely on qubit shuttling, understanding decoherence of the shuttled multi-spin qubits becomes crucial. We analyze fidelity and leakage of the logical qubits dephased by the spatio-temporally correlated 1/f noise, considering two-, three-, and four-spin encodings. We study different shuttling protocols and establish that for all encodings generally, parallel shuttling provides the best protection against decoherence at short distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms others for long-range transport (although the exact boundaries depend on the specific device parameters). We explain this common behavior in terms of the dephasing factors of pairs of the shuttled spins; we provide explicit expressions for fidelities and leakage, thus enabling experimentalists to predict performance of the multi-spin qubits from only several independently measured pairwise dephasing factors. Our results establish a connection between shuttling trajectories, noise correlations, and qubit decoherence, and provide guidance for achieving noise-resilient shuttling in scalable semiconductor quantum processors.

articles.title: Thermodynamics of Speed and Efficiency with Quantum Feedback
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08564v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rapid thermodynamic operations generally entail irreversible dissipation, giving rise to trade-offs between operating speed and thermodynamic cost. Yet, how quantum feedback fundamentally reshapes these trade-offs remains elusive. Here, we derive a finite-time current--dissipation relation for continuously monitored open quantum dynamics with jump feedback. From this fundamental relation, we establish a quantum speed limit and a power-efficiency trade-off for stationary information engines, identifying how feedback affects state transformations and the performance of engines through both informational entropy and direct dynamical contributions. Our results provide a quantitative foundation for fast, low-dissipation quantum thermodynamics in the presence of feedback control, exemplified by attaining the generalized Landauer bound in finite-time information erasure and approaching unit information efficiency at finite power in the large-system limit of a collective engine.

articles.title: Deep-UV All-dielectric qBIC Metasurface for Refractive Index Sensing
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08733v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: All-dielectric metasurfaces supporting quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBICs) have emerged as powerful platforms for biosensing, yet their operation remains largely concentrated in the visible and near-infrared regimes. Extending these resonances into the deep-ultraviolet (DUV) to probe the intrinsic electronic absorption of biomolecules presents substantial material and nanofabrication challenges. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a hafnium dioxide (HfO₂) metasurface supporting DUV qBICs in the wavelength range from 225 nm to 340 nm with quality factors reaching 500. We further demonstrate its refractive index sensing capabilities through integration with a microfluidic cell and optical characterization in reflection mode. We show that the introduction of an aqueous buffer leads to a further quality factor enhancement. Achieving a sensitivity of up to approximately 60 nm/RIU and an operational figure of merit of 40 RIU⁻¹, this low-loss HfO₂ metasurface provides a robust foundation for label-free DUV biosensing.

articles.title: Electrohydrodynamic interactions of two Quincke rotors: asymptotic theory and boundary element simulations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08807v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Weakly conducting spheres suspended in a leaky dielectric fluid can undergo spontaneous Quincke rotation when the applied electric field exceeds a critical value. We investigate how electric and hydrodynamic interactions modify this instability and the subsequent rotation of two spheres at fixed separation and orientation. Starting from electric dipole and hydrodynamic rotlet interactions, we develop a systematic far-field asymptotic theory. Away from onset, slow drift of the rotation axes makes a regular expansion fail at long times. A multiple-scale expansion gives slow phase equations that select the axes according to pair orientation and field strength. Near onset, weak interactions produce corrections comparable to the isolated rotation magnitude. A detuned multiple-scale expansion gives coupled equations for the transverse dipole amplitudes. Their linearization identifies four collective rotation modes, whose critical fields and steady branches with one active mode are determined together with their stability. At leading order near onset, electric interaction shifts all four modal thresholds equally, whereas hydrodynamic interaction makes counter-rotation appear first for pair angles below cos⁻¹(1/sqrt3)simeq54.7^circ and co-rotation above it. Away from onset, the angle separating stable counter-rotation from stable co-rotation increases with field strength. Boundary element method (BEM) simulations place onset within a field interval for each configuration and resolve the growth and relaxation of rotation. Steady-speed comparisons show how pair orientation changes the balance between electric and hydrodynamic effects. We compare the unexpanded dipole-rotlet model of Das and Saintillan [Phys. Rev. E 87, 043014 (2013)] with our asymptotic theory and BEM simulations.

articles.title: Optimal asymptotic pure-state conversion under thermal operations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08974v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum thermodynamics seeks to characterize possible state transformations under thermodynamic constraints in microscopic quantum systems. In the fully quantum regime, however, quantum coherence imposes various restrictions on state conversions, and a complete characterization of state convertibility has remained open. Here we resolve this problem for asymptotic conversions between pure states. Specifically, we show that asymptotic convertibility is fully determined by the free-energy and energy-variance ratios. Our result reveals how genuinely quantum effects quantitatively constrain state conversions in quantum thermodynamics.

articles.title: Continuum mean-field theory of spatiotemporal pattern formation in a three-state active Potts model
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09180v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the spatiotemporal dynamics of a three-state active Potts model with a cyclic transition bias. Starting from microscopic Glauber-type dynamics, we derive macroscopic continuum field equations through a spatial mean-field approximation. Linear stability and weakly nonlinear analyses reveal that increasing the coupling strength induces a Hopf bifurcation, near which the critical amplitude dynamics is described by the complex Ginzburg--Landau equation. In the spatially homogeneous limit, the system exhibits limit-cycle oscillations and ordered states, with an intermediate regime of bistability bounded by a Z₃-symmetric heteroclinic bifurcation. In two dimensions, the system sustains stable rotating spiral waves. Using perturbation theory based on one-dimensional traveling fronts, we semianalytically predict the curvature-dependent propagation velocity of circular fronts, as well as the rotational angular velocity and pitch of spiral waves. Finally, we compare the continuum model with discrete Monte Carlo simulations to clarify the role of thermal fluctuations and evaluate the validity of the mean-field approximation.

articles.title: Increased Crystal Nucleation in the Glassy State of a Polymer/Water Mixture
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09456v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Within classical nucleation theory, crystal nucleation requires sufficient supersaturation, but is suppressed at low temperatures due to reduced molecular mobility, leading to a maximum nucleation rate typically above the glass transition temperature T_g. Here, we experimentally show that this conventional picture breaks down in a biocompatible polymer poly(2-methoxyethyl acrylate)(PMEA)/water mixture. We find that the number of nuclei increases dramatically below T_g, with the effective nucleation rate exhibiting an unusual maximum at approximately T_g-10 K. Calorimetric experiments reveal a strong temperature-history dependence of cold crystallization of water in hydrated PMEA, which is explained by the observed nucleation behavior. We propose that the unusual enhancement of nucleation below T_g provides a key mechanism linking high glass-forming ability and cold crystallization upon heating, thereby explaining the striking asymmetry in crystallization behavior between cooling and heating. Our findings suggest that a hidden nucleation-rate maximum below T_g may also underlie cold crystallization in other glass-forming liquids.

articles.title: Arrival-time problem in the quantum information era - observation of a Zeno crossover in monitored arrival-time distributions
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09814v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When does a quantum particle arrive at a detector? The temporal distributions of itinerant quantum particles have been debated since the birth of quantum mechanics. Here we study the arrival-time problem in periodically monitored spin chains and quantum circuits. The arrival dynamics exhibits two regimes, the quantum Zeno and the low-monitoring regime, separated by an optimal monitoring period set by the single-particle bandwidth. In support of the theory, on superconducting quantum hardware, we measure arrival-time distributions for single and multiple interacting particles in one- and two-dimensional circuits. The measured distributions resolve both regimes and agree closely with quantum-trajectory theory. The crossover persists in interacting many-particle systems: the optimal monitoring point is preserved while many-body interference reshapes the distributions. Zeno suppression likewise persists in two-dimensional geometry. Together, these results show that the two regimes are a generic feature of monitored propagation rather than a single-particle effect. To our knowledge, our work constitutes the first experimental measurement of arrival-time distributions in a monitored quantum transport setting, addressing one of the longest-standing problems in quantum mechanics.

articles.title: Numerical investigation of the equilibrium Kauzmann transition in a two-dimensional atomistic glass
articles.abstract: arXiv:2507.03590v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dense liquids gradually transform into non-equilibrium amorphous solids as they pass through the experimental glass transition. Experimentally, ergodicity is lost because measurements are conducted within a finite time window. More than seventy years ago, Kauzmann posed a fundamental question: If experiments could run indefinitely, would there exist a critical temperature at which an ergodicity-breaking phase transition occurs? Random first-order transitions represent the modern theoretical framework for this idea. However, theoretical calculations in finite dimensions are challenging, whereas experimental and numerical limitations on accessible timescales hinder direct observation of the putative Kauzmann transition. Here, we overcome this longstanding barrier by developing a computational strategy that properly combines three Monte Carlo methods to access the desired equilibrium thermodynamic properties of a two-dimensional atomistic glass-former down to zero temperature across a range of system sizes up to 77 particles. This enables us to directly measure thermodynamic and structural observables that provide unambiguous evidence that the system undergoes a finite-size version of the Kauzmann transition at a temperature that is much lower than other energy scales and decreases rapidly with system size, thus suggesting the existence of a zero-temperature Kauzmann transition for two-dimensional glasses. The transition is towards an ideal glass state characterized by a complex energy landscape and a hierarchical organization of low-lying states.

articles.title: Transport and thermalization under noncommuting localized constraints
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.23781v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the effects of spatially localized conserved quantities on transport and thermalization in quantum and classical many-body systems. We consider several related models: the integrable quantum Volterra model, its nonintegrable classical limit, and two cellular automata derived from the latter. Although localized constraints are often associated with lattice gauge theories, our models do not admit such an interpretation. In systems with discrete degrees of freedom, these constraints induce uniform fragmentation of the Hilbert or configuration space. In the quantum Volterra model, we derive an exact mapping of the dynamics within each Hilbert-space fragment onto a quantum chiral Potts chain. We find that energy transport is ballistic, with identical transport coefficients across all fragments. In the nonintegrable classical limit, energy transport is diffusive, and we similarly find the diffusion constant to be independent of whether or not the constraints are fixed (resolved). Finally, in the cellular automata, we show that, despite leaving transport unaffected, localized constraints lead to a strong breakdown of local ergodicity.

articles.title: Limit cycles in periodically driven open quantum systems
articles.abstract: arXiv:1908.03900v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate the long-time behavior of quantum N-level systems that are coupled to a Markovian environment and subject to periodic driving. As our main result, we obtain a general algebraic condition ensuring that all solutions of a periodic quantum master equation with Lindblad form approach a unique limit cycle. Quite intuitively, this criterion requires that the dissipative terms of the master equation connect all subspaces of the system Hilbert space during an arbitrarily small fraction of the cycle time. Our results provide a natural extension of Spohn's algebraic condition for the approach to equilibrium to systems with external driving.

articles.title: Concentration of ergotropy in quantum many-body systems
articles.abstract: arXiv:2412.19801v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ergotropyunicodex2014the maximal amount of unitarily extractable workunicodex2014quantifies the "charge level" of a quantum battery. We prove that, in large many-body batteries, it exhibits a concentration of measure phenomenon. Namely, the ergotropy almost coincides with its average for almost all states sampled from the Hilbertunicodex2013Schmidt measure. Importantly, the average ergotropy is macroscopic, scaling with the number of particles in the system. This occurs despite the von Neumann entropy also concentrating around a macroscopic average, a surprising coexistence since high entropy is commonly associated with effective thermality and thus passivity. We establish these results by proving that ergotropy, as a function of the state, is Lipschitz continuous with respect to the Bures distance and by applying Lévy's measure concentration lemma. Furthermore, we numerically extend our findings to the Bures measure, which represents the situation with the least amount of prior information about the state. Our continuity and concentration bounds open a new perspective on the noise-robustness of quantum many-body batteries and lay the groundwork for further rigorous studies of their charge stability and work extraction with limited prior knowledge.

articles.title: Statistics of Strongly Coupled Defects in Superconducting Qubits
articles.abstract: arXiv:2506.00193v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Decoherence in superconducting qubits is dominated by defects that reside at amorphous interfaces. Interaction with discrete defects results in dropouts that complicate qubit operation and lead to nongaussian tails in the distribution of qubit energy relaxation time T₁ that degrade system performance. Spectral diffusion of defects over time leads to fluctuations in T₁, posing a challenge for calibration. In this work, we measure the energy relaxation of flux-tunable transmons over a range of operating frequencies. We vary qubit geometry to change the interface participation ratio by more than an order of magnitude. Our results are consistent with loss dominated by discrete interfacial defects. Moreover, we are able to localize the dominant defects to within 500 nm of the qubit junctions, where residues from liftoff are present. These results motivate new approaches to qubit junction fabrication that avoid the residues intrinsic to the liftoff process.

articles.title: Imprints of information scrambling on eigenstates of a quantum chaotic system
articles.abstract: arXiv:2507.02853v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: How are the spatial and temporal patterns of information scrambling in locally interacting quantum many-body systems imprinted on the eigenstates of the system's time-evolution operator? We address this question by identifying statistical correlations among sets of minimally four eigenstates that provide a unified framework for various measures of information scrambling. These include operator mutual information and operator entanglement entropy of the time-evolution operator, as well as more conventional diagnostics such as two-point dynamical correlations and out-of-time-ordered correlators. We demonstrate this framework by deriving exact results for eigenstate correlations in a minimal model of quantum chaos -- Floquet dual-unitary circuits. These results reveal not only the butterfly effect and the information lightcone, but also finer structures of scrambling within the lightcone. Our work thus shows how the eigenstates of a chaotic system can encode the full spatiotemporal anatomy of quantum chaos, going beyond the descriptions offered by random matrix theory and the eigenstate thermalisation hypothesis.

articles.title: Framing Anomaly in Lattice Chern-Simons-Maxwell Theory
articles.abstract: arXiv:2601.04318v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Framing anomaly is a key property of (2+1)d chiral topological orders, for it reveals that the chirality is an intrinsic bulk property of the system, rather than a property of the boundary between two systems. Understanding framing anomaly in lattice models is particularly interesting, as concrete, solvable lattice models of chiral topological orders are rare. In a previous work, we defined and solved the U(1) Chern-Simons-Maxwell theory on spacetime lattice, showing its chiral edge mode and the associated gravitational anomaly on boundary. In this work, we show its framing anomaly in the absence of boundary, by computing the expectation of a lattice version of the modular T operator in the ground subspace on a spatial torus, from which we extract that langle T rangle has a universal phase of -2π/12 as expected: -2π/8 from the Gauss-Milgram sum of the topological spins of the ground states, and 2π/24 from the framing anomaly; we can also extract the 2π/24 framing anomaly phase alone from the full spectrum of T in the ground subspace by computing langle T^m rangle. This pins down the last and most crucial property required for a valid lattice definition of U(1) Chern-Simons theory.

articles.title: Quantum error mitigation from information dynamics
articles.abstract: arXiv:2609.31934v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Overcoming experimental errors is a central challenge in quantum science. This challenge is particularly acute in large and complex quantum circuits, where quantum information spreads into exponentially many paths, foiling any direct attempt to understand errors' impact. In this work, we present a novel approach to understanding and mitigating experimental errors, based on a surprisingly compact representation of a quantum circuit's information dynamics, the reactivity function. The shape of a circuit's reactivity function governs its noise response, and its amenability to different error mitigation methods. From this viewpoint, we introduce two complementary such methods. The first, Pauli-path zero-noise extrapolation, fits a parameterized model to a circuit's reactivity function and uses it to accurately extrapolate to zero noise. The second, tunable error cancellation, filters a circuit's reactivity function to cancel noise on all information up to a threshold locality. Crucially, both methods feature a tuning parameter that allows one to systematically improve their accuracy until convergence. Across three circuit families from published experiments, our methods overcome conventional zero-noise extrapolation biases as large as 30%; at sim10⁻² root-mean-square error, they reduce sampling cost relative to probabilistic error cancellation by up to a factor of 10³.

articles.title: How balloons lose their charge by collecting ions from the air
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The air we breathe contains radioactive particles. Each time one of these particles decays, it creates hundreds of thousands of ionized air molecules. These ions make the air conductive, which is one reason insulated surfaces lose charge over time. Here we observe the discharge of two statically charged balloons by measuring the repulsive force between them over time. The initial rates of charge loss are relatively large, especially at higher humidities. This large rate of charge loss is likely dominated by the emission of water ions from the balloons surface. Approximately 1 hour after charging, the charge loss rates are much smaller and agree with predictions calculated from the radon concentration in the air and the size of the room, for reasonable aerosol concentrations.

articles.title: An Analytical Model for Laser-Activated Two-Phase Choking and Microfluidic Suction on Surface Boundary Layers
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a predictive fluid mechanics model to calculate pressure drops (0.25 atm) and fluid velocities (2.50 m/s) governed by localized phase change and choking phenomena in a capillary-constrained, coaxial microfluidic actuator. Driven by near-infrared thermal absorption, the analytical framework describes how energy deposition drives vapor cavity growth and subsequent cavitation bubble collapse, inducing a transient suction force across a curved, two-radii Young-Laplace capillary boundary. Velocity drops are derived from closed-form analytical equations that explicitly couple vapor volume dynamics with non-linear flow area restriction and fluid drag. The model predicts a maximum boundary layer wall shear stress of 30.06 Pa at the target interface. Crucially, this shear magnitude matches the physical threshold required to mechanically strip surface contaminant boundary layers while remaining below the damage threshold of underlying target substrates. Finally, we formulate a closed-form expression for the maximum allowable liquid inlet temperature required to prevent thermal saturation and sustain stable, continuous microfluidic suction cycles. These equations establish direct engineering design rules for optimizing phase-change microfluidic actuators and next-generation coaxial fluidic systems.

articles.title: Immobilisation and remobilisation of surfactant-covered drop interfaces in electric fields: Simulations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08750v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fluid--fluid interfaces are seldom clean due to the presence of surfactants, which can strongly modify their dynamics. Interfacial flow redistributes surfactant, creating concentration gradients whose Marangoni stresses can immobilise the interface. By contrast, surface diffusion or exchange with the bulk can reduce these gradients and restore interfacial motion. We study this competition using a two-dimensional model of a surfactant-covered leaky-dielectric drop in a uniform electric field. Electric stresses drive the classical Taylor circulation, in which the drop remains non-rotating. At stronger fields, convection of interfacial charge can destabilise this state and produce the Quincke regime, characterised by spontaneous mean rotation. Using a fully nonlinear model on a fixed circular interface, we show that weak surfactant diffusion allows Marangoni stresses to suppress the Taylor circulation almost completely. Quincke rotation remobilises this nearly arrested interface and restores a substantial straining circulation, whose orientation varies with the applied field. Surfactant also shifts the critical field for rotation and can change the onset from subcritical to supercritical. Surface diffusion and exchange with a well-mixed bulk reservoir can produce similar flow responses and rotation thresholds despite different surfactant distributions. The spatial variation of surfactant concentration therefore provides additional information for distinguishing the two transport mechanisms.

articles.title: Laser-Direct-Written polymer WGM microring laser integrated on a fiber tip for refractive index sensing
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.08805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) microlasers are promising for refractometric sensing, but their practical implementation can be limited by the need for stable resonator-coupler alignment. Here, we demonstrate a Rhodamine B-doped polymer WGM microring laser directly fabricated on an optical-fiber tip, eliminating the external resonator-fiber coupling interface at the sensing head. Micro-droplet coating and UV laser direct writing are combined for fabrication, while finite-difference time-domain simulations guide the microring laser design. The microlasers operate in air and water with thresholds of 0.224 uJ and 0.458 uJ, respectively. Refractometric measurements in aqueous glucose solutions yield a bulk refractive index sensitivity of 364.95 nm/RIU and a detection limit of 2.47 x 10⁽⁻⁴⁾ RIU. Water-induced polymer changes and photobleaching are also investigated. This fiber-tip architecture provides a basis for probe-based refractometric sensing in environmental and biochemical applications.

articles.title: Domain-Adapted Deep Optical Flow for Multiphase Velocimetry in Unsteady Cloud Cavitation
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-resolved velocimetry inside cloud cavitation remains a fundamental measurement problem. Particle image velocimetry (PIV) requires uniform tracer seeding and undistorted particle images, and cavitating flow violates both, because tracers do not penetrate vapor structures and refractive index mismatch across deforming interfaces produces spurious vectors. We present a domain-adapted deep optical flow framework for two-phase velocimetry, built on a Recurrent All-Pairs Field Transforms (RAFT) architecture fine-tuned on synthetic image pairs rendered from multiphase OpenFOAM simulations (RAFT-CloudCav). It is evaluated against a pre-trained generalist RAFT model, Farnebäck and OpenPIV on 130,000 frames/s recordings of a Venturi test section at 30 and 48 L/min. As no experimental ground truth exists, validation uses three quantities that require none, namely the integrated flow rate against a turbine meter, the liquid-phase velocity divergence, which mass conservation requires to vanish, and the station-to-station spread of the flow rate. RAFT-CloudCav recovers 47.75 L/min against a metered 48.0 ± 0.5 L/min, the closest of the four methods, and its flow rate varies by 2.0% across four streamwise stations, versus 6-7% for the classical methods. It returns a coherent near-wall reverse flow of -0.71 m/s, the time-averaged signature of the upstream-propagating re-entrant jet, where OpenPIV returns none. In the non-cavitating control, at 51 μm/pixel only three grid points fall inside a 0.68 mm boundary layer and the peak wall-normal gradient is under-predicted more than thirtyfold, while 13 and 19 μm/pixel agree with each other. The mean field is recovered without tracer particles at roughly three times the per-frame uncertainty. Uncertainties are estimated a posteriori from the image residual and propagated conservatively.

articles.title: Low-Rank Iteration for Efficient Calculations of Topological Surface States
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surface states are hallmarks of topological phases, and their efficient computation is crucial for topology characterization. Conventional supercell methods (SCM) approximate semi-infinite systems as finite periodic ones, but suffer from high computational cost, artificial inter-surface coupling, and slow convergence near band edges. Recently, boundary problems for semi-infinite systems have been recast as block-tridiagonal equations and solved by the cyclic reduction method (CRM) and the transfer matrix method (TMM). However, these approaches remain resource-intensive, as fine-mesh discretization produces very large matrices. Recognizing the intrinsic sparsity and low rank of these matrices, we develop a low-rank iterative method (LIM) with stochastic trace estimation that substantially reduces complexity and memory without sacrificing accuracy, while remaining straightforwardly parallelizable. Benchmarks on 2D and 3D topological systems show orders-of-magnitude acceleration over CRM and TMM. LIM extends readily to heterostructures, defective interfaces, and non-Hermitian systems, providing an efficient platform for topological and plasmonic surface phenomena.

articles.title: When is an Optical Design Problem a Mass Transfer Problem?
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates whether optical design problems can be represented as Monge--Kantorovich mass transfer problems with some cost function. An optical problem is specified by a function defining a particular family of supporting surfaces for the optical element. We introduce the notion of geometric equivalence between optical and transport problems, which is directly related to the possibility of formulating an optical design problem as a mass transfer problem. A necessary condition for such equivalence is derived in the semi-discrete setting. It allows a transport representation to be ruled out without choosing a cost function in advance. The condition is applied to the near-field refractor problem and to the design of two refracting surfaces transforming a spherical beam into a spherical or collimated beam. For these problems, the necessary condition is shown to fail in physically admissible configurations. We also study an optical element with a single working surface and an arbitrary regular incident wavefront. In the far field, geometric equivalence to a mass transfer problem requires a planar or spherical wavefront, whereas in the near field with a planar target, the necessary condition fails for an arbitrary smooth wavefront.

articles.title: Independent nuclear charge radius determinations: bound-electron g factor versus muonic atom spectroscopy
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an alternative method to determine absolute nuclear charge radii competitively via the bound electron g factor of H-like ions. The method is demonstrated for ¹¹⁸Sn by extracting its radius with a precision of 0.1%. This is the second most precise radius ever determined from an electronic system. We benchmark our result against a state-of-the-art value derived from the spectrum of muonic ¹¹⁸Sn. This comparison reveals a 3.2σ tension, prompting a careful reexamination of the calculations and calling for additional measurements. Crucially, after decades, we now have two independent methods to measure absolute charge radii with similar precision.

articles.title: Absolute Calibration of a Broadband Transmission Grating Spectrometer from 5 to 400 nm with Uncertainty Estimates
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the absolute calibration of a transmission grating spectrometer (TGS) with uncertainty estimates in the 5--400 nm range using synchrotron radiation at the BEAR beamline at Elettra light source in Trieste, Italy. Firstly, the spectral responsivity of a Si photodiode in the spectrometer was absolutely calibrated with respect to the absolutely-calibrated beamline photodiode. Subsequently, this photodiode was used to calibrate the transmittance of Zr and Al thin-film filters, along with bulk MgF₂ and UV-grade fused silica windows at their operating positions in the spectrometer to minimize mounting-induced uncertainties. Next, the quantum efficiency of the spectrometer's CCD camera was calibrated over the 5--400 nm range. Lastly, three gratings with line densities of 10000, 3000, and 1000 lines/mm were calibrated for spectroscopy in the ranges extending from soft X-ray to extreme-, vacuum- and deep-ultraviolet (DUV) wavelengths, respectively. The combination of various filters and gratings enables absolutely calibrated spectroscopy with high versatility across a broad wavelength range from soft X-rays to DUV.

articles.title: RainFlow: Flow Matching for Infrared-Only Quantitative Precipitation Estimation
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geostationary infrared imagers observe precipitating systems every 10 to 15 minutes over large areas, but they sense cloud tops rather than the rain beneath. Their brightness temperatures constrain surface rain only weakly, so retrievals trained by regression return a smooth estimate that misses heavy rain and carries no measure of uncertainty. We treat infrared-only retrieval as conditional generation and introduce RainFlow, a flow-matching model that generates ensembles of rain fields from MSG/SEVIRI infrared observations, in a direct and a residual variant. Evaluated against radar over metropolitan France for a full year, the generated members are realistic rain fields, with the observed dry areas, heavy rain and spatial structure, and the ensemble mean is as accurate as a deterministic baseline. Used as probabilities, the ensembles locate heavy rain at scales where the baseline has no skill, and their spread captures most of the retrieval error, with only slight underdispersion. Trained with a time-sampling density that favours the noise end of the generative trajectory, the two variants reach similar skill. The direct variant depends strongly on this choice of density, whereas the residual variant is nearly insensitive to it. Evaluating the generated rain as a function of brightness temperature shows that the ensembles reproduce how rain depends on it over most of the range. It also isolates the remaining gap, an underestimate of both the amount and the variability of rain under the coldest cloud tops, which scores computed over all pixels do not reveal.

articles.title: Spin to Orbital Angular Momentum Conversion in the Neutron Nucleus Weak Interaction
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The neutron nucleus weak interaction generates a small parity non conserving rotation of the neutron spin as the neutron moves through matter. This parity-odd neutron rotary power can reach up to 2.2e-3 rad * cm-1 for slow neutrons in 139La, which possesses a p-wave resonance at 0.7 eV where the parity-odd asymmetry is greatly amplified. This spin rotation must conserve total angular momentum. Here we show that this conservation occurs through neutron orbital angular momentum generation. We experimentally demonstrate that a neutron prepared initially in a longitudinal spin-orbit state experiences no change in total angular momentum.

articles.title: Vertically-coupled microring resonators for lithium niobate on insulator integrated photonics
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose and demonstrate lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) microring resonators that are verticallycoupled to index-matched silicon-rich silicon nitride (SiN x ) access waveguides as an alternative to conventional lateral coupling schemes for integrated photonics applications. The wafer-scalable fabrication process involves a planarization step exploiting a single-step and reproducible spin-coating of a SU-8 epoxy spacer layer which allows a controlled separation to be established between the resonator and its access waveguide. The resulting multimode and single-mode microring resonators exhibit, for their fundamental TE 0 mode, intrinsic quality factors of 4.0 x 10 5 and 3.4 x 10 5 , respectively.

articles.title: Time-gated optical-parametric-amplification and field-resolved detection of mid-infrared free-induction decay signals
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.09783v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Infrared spectroscopy is a key tool to study complex structural dynamics in molecular systems. However, resolving weak or broad vibrational modes is challenging due to their rapid decay. Here, we demonstrate a technique to significantly extend the detectable lifetime - and thereby spectral resolution - of molecular signatures by employing synchronized time-gated optical parametric amplification of mid-infrared free-induction decay signals. Utilizing a Cr:ZnS laser system and a nonlinear ZnGeP2 crystal, we achieve a 10-fold increase in the electric field strength of the infrared molecular signal, yielding a two-orders of magnitude enhancement in dynamic range and a 2-fold increase in the signal-to-noise ratio. Using isopropyl alcohol as a model system, we demonstrate that OPA-enhanced detection extends the observable window of vibrational modes up to 72 %.
